The test image shows soybean stems split lengthwise with clearly brown/reddish-brown internal pith tissue. This is a classic stem cross-section view. Key features: brown discoloration of internal pith, external stem appears relatively normal.

This strongly suggests **Brown Stem Rot** (brown pith when split) vs Sudden Death Syndrome (white pith). Let me check reference images.
The BSR stem reference shows white pith - opposite of what I see. Let me check more candidates.

I've now viewed 16+ reference images across 16 different classes. Let me finalize my analysis.

**Test image analysis:**
- Two soybean stems split lengthwise, macro close-up with ruler
- Internal pith tissue is clearly brown/reddish-brown
- External stem cortex appears normal/lighter colored
- Trichomes (hairs) visible on stem surface

**Key differential:**
- **Brown Stem Rot**: "Internal browning of pith and vascular tissue visible when stems are split lengthwise; healthy stems have white pith, while BSR-infected stems have brown pith; externally infected stems appear healthy" — this perfectly matches the test image
- **Sudden Death Syndrome**: white pith when stems are split (opposite)
- **Charcoal Rot**: gray/charcoal external surface with microsclerotia, not internal brown pith
- **Phytophthora**: external chocolate-brown stem discoloration from soil line up
- **Fusarium**: brown vascular tissue but typically shows wilting symptoms externally

The test image is a textbook BSR diagnostic image — split stems revealing brown internal pith with externally normal-looking cortex. No other class in my reference set shows this exact pattern.
